chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr from Hanan ibn Sadir who said:

We entered upon Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and with us was Farqad the cupper. He said: 'I am your ransom, I perform a deed and I have asked about it more than one and two people, and they claimed it is a disliked deed. And I love to ask you, so if it is disliked I will cease from it and perform other deeds, for I will adhere in that to your word.' He said: 'And what is it?' He said: 'The cupper.' He said: 'Eat from your earnings, O son of my brother, and give in charity, and perform Hajj from it, and marry, for indeed the Prophet of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) had himself cupped and gave the reward, and if it were forbidden he would not have given it.'

He said: 'May Allah make me your ransom, I have a male camel that I rent out, so what do you say about its earnings?' He said: 'Eat from its earnings, for it is lawful for you, and the people dislike it.'
Hanan said: 'I said: For what reason do they dislike it while it is lawful?' He said: 'For the people's taunting of one another.'

key_terms.مَكْرُوهٌ: Disliked (a legal status between permissible and forbidden)

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on the earnings of a cupper or renting out animals if the public dislikes it?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) distinguishes between legal permissibility (halal) and social preference (makruh li-ghayrihi), ruling that a cupper’s earnings are lawful despite public dislike, justified by the Prophet’s precedent of paying for cupping. He further extends this principle to the earnings from renting a male camel, noting that the dislike stems not from the transaction itself but from the social custom of using camels for taunting (ta’ir). This highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on separating intrinsic legality from extrinsic social customs.
